Using NetworkX

Dataset: The Twitch Streamer Social Network (MUSAE) was collected and published by Benedek Rozemberczki, Carl Allen, and Rik Sarkar (2021). It consists of mutual friendship graphs among Twitch streamers in multiple language communities, with node attributes including total channel views, days active, partnership status, and a mature content flag. Published in: Rozemberczki, B., Allen, C., and Sarkar, R. (2021). “Multi-Scale Attributed Node Embedding.” Journal of Complex Networks, 9(2).

Download: Navigate to the MUSAE GitHub repository: https://github.com/benedekrozemberczki/MUSAE. Under input/dataset/, download three files for the English-language community: musae_ENGB_edges.csv, musae_ENGB_features.json, and musae_ENGB_target.csv. Save all three to your working directory.

Analytical focus: This session treats the Twitch friendship network as a model information environment. Streamers are actors; friendships are the channels through which trends, content, and influence flow. The central questions are: who can spread information most effectively, how far does information travel from different starting points, and what structural features — community membership, bridge positions, attribute wealth — best predict influence capacity.

Deliverable: This completed worksheet plus one exported figure. Due at end of class.

Part 1 (10 min) · Load Data and Build the Graph

Goal: Load the English-language Twitch streamer network and attach node attributes. Understand what each attribute means before computing any metrics — the attributes are your ground-truth measures of real-world influence against which structural measures will be compared.

Step 2 — Build the NetworkX Graph with Attributes

# Build undirected graph
G = nx.from_pandas_edgelist(edges, source='from', target='to')

# Attach node attributes from target file
# Typical columns: id, views, mature, partner, new_id, days, language
for _, row in target.iterrows():
    node_id = int(row['new_id']) if 'new_id' in target.columns \
              else int(row['id'])
    if G.has_node(node_id):
        G.nodes[node_id]['views']    = int(row.get('views', 0))
        G.nodes[node_id]['partner']  = int(row.get('partner', 0))
        G.nodes[node_id]['mature']   = int(row.get('mature', 0))
        G.nodes[node_id]['days']     = int(row.get('days', 0))

print(f"Nodes: {G.number_of_nodes()}")
print(f"Edges: {G.number_of_edges()}")
print(f"Connected: {nx.is_connected(G)}")
print(f"Components: {nx.number_connected_components(G)}")
print(f"Density: {nx.density(G):.6f}")

Part 3 (12 min) · Information Diffusion Simulation

Goal: Simulate how information spreads through the Twitch friendship network using the Independent Cascade (IC) model. In the IC model, each infected node has one chance to infect each uninfected neighbor with probability \(p\). Compare the spread from strategically selected seed nodes (high structural influence) vs. randomly selected seeds. This operationalizes the influence maximization problem: given a fixed number of “seeds” (initial spreaders), which actors should you activate to maximize total reach?

Step 8 — Implement the Independent Cascade Model

def independent_cascade(G, seeds, p=0.05, n_trials=200):
    """
    Simulate the Independent Cascade model.

    Parameters
    ----------
    G       : NetworkX graph
    seeds   : list of seed nodes (initially infected)
    p       : transmission probability per edge
    n_trials: number of Monte Carlo trials to average

    Returns
    -------
    mean_infected : average total nodes infected across trials
    std_infected  : standard deviation
    """
    trial_results = []
    for _ in range(n_trials):
        infected    = set(seeds)
        frontier    = set(seeds)
        while frontier:
            new_frontier = set()
            for node in frontier:
                for neighbor in G.neighbors(node):
                    if neighbor not in infected:
                        if random.random() < p:
                            new_frontier.add(neighbor)
            infected  |= new_frontier
            frontier   = new_frontier
        trial_results.append(len(infected))
    return np.mean(trial_results), np.std(trial_results)


# Test with a single high-degree node
top_node = top10_deg[0][0]
mean_inf, std_inf = independent_cascade(G, seeds=[top_node], p=0.05)
print(f"Single seed (top degree node {top_node}):")
print(f"  Mean infected: {mean_inf:.1f} / {G.number_of_nodes()} nodes")
print(f"  Spread rate:   {100*mean_inf/G.number_of_nodes():.2f}%")

Step 9 — Compare Seeding Strategies

# Work on the largest connected component for cleaner results
lcc_nodes = max(nx.connected_components(G), key=len)
G_lcc     = G.subgraph(lcc_nodes).copy()
print(f"LCC size: {G_lcc.number_of_nodes()} nodes, "
      f"{G_lcc.number_of_edges()} edges")

N_SEEDS = 10   # number of initial spreaders
P_TRANS = 0.05 # transmission probability

# Recompute measures on LCC
deg_lcc  = dict(G_lcc.degree())
pr_lcc   = nx.pagerank(G_lcc, alpha=0.85)
core_lcc = nx.core_number(G_lcc)

# Select seeds by each strategy (top-N nodes)
seeds_deg  = [n for n, _ in sorted(deg_lcc.items(),
               key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)[:N_SEEDS]]
seeds_pr   = [n for n, _ in sorted(pr_lcc.items(),
               key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)[:N_SEEDS]]
seeds_core = sorted(core_lcc, key=core_lcc.get,
                    reverse=True)[:N_SEEDS]
seeds_rand = random.sample(list(G_lcc.nodes()), N_SEEDS)

strategies = {
    'Degree (top-10)':    seeds_deg,
    'PageRank (top-10)':  seeds_pr,
    'K-core (top-10)':    seeds_core,
    'Random (10 nodes)':  seeds_rand,
}

print(f"\n{'Strategy':<25} {'Mean infected':>14} {'Std':>8} "
      f"{'% of LCC':>10}")
print('-' * 62)
results = {}
for name, seeds in strategies.items():
    mean, std = independent_cascade(G_lcc, seeds, p=P_TRANS)
    pct = 100 * mean / G_lcc.number_of_nodes()
    results[name] = (mean, std, pct)
    print(f"{name:<25} {mean:>14.1f} {std:>8.1f} {pct:>9.2f}%")

Part 4 (8 min) · Community Structure and Influence Containment

Goal: Detect communities in the Twitch network and assess whether community structure acts as a containment barrier for information flow — trapping cascades within communities — or a highway that accelerates intra-community spread. In information operations, strong community structure implies that narratives may be highly effective within a target community but fail to cross into adjacent ones without specific bridge actors.

Step 12 — Detect Communities

from networkx.algorithms import community

comms = list(community.greedy_modularity_communities(G_lcc))
comms.sort(key=len, reverse=True)

mod = nx.community.modularity(G_lcc, comms)
print(f"Communities found: {len(comms)}")
print(f"Modularity: {mod:.4f}")
print()

# Assign community IDs
node_comm = {}
for i, comm in enumerate(comms):
    for n in comm:
        node_comm[n] = i

print(f"{'Comm':>5} {'Size':>7} {'Avg degree':>12} "
      f"{'Partner rate':>13} {'Median views':>14}")
print('-' * 58)
for i, comm in enumerate(comms[:8]):
    comm = list(comm)
    avg_d  = np.mean([deg_lcc.get(n, 0) for n in comm])
    p_rate = np.mean([G_lcc.nodes[n].get('partner', 0) for n in comm])
    m_view = int(np.median([G_lcc.nodes[n].get('views', 0) for n in comm]))
    print(f"{i+1:5d} {len(comm):7d} {avg_d:12.2f} "
          f"{p_rate:13.3f} {m_view:14,}")

Step 13 — Intra-Community vs. Cross-Community Spread

def cascade_community_breakdown(G, seeds, node_comm, p=0.05,
                                n_trials=100):
    """
    Run IC model and report fraction of infections that land
    within the same community as the seeds vs. in other communities.
    """
    seed_comm = set(node_comm.get(s, -1) for s in seeds)
    within, outside = [], []

    for _ in range(n_trials):
        infected = set(seeds)
        frontier = set(seeds)
        while frontier:
            new_f = set()
            for node in frontier:
                for nb in G.neighbors(node):
                    if nb not in infected and random.random() < p:
                        new_f.add(nb)
            infected |= new_f
            frontier  = new_f

        w = sum(1 for n in infected
                if node_comm.get(n, -1) in seed_comm)
        o = len(infected) - w
        within.append(w)
        outside.append(o)

    return np.mean(within), np.mean(outside)


# Use top-3 community's top-degree node as seed
comm0_nodes = [n for n, c in node_comm.items() if c == 0]
seed_intra  = [max(comm0_nodes, key=lambda n: deg_lcc.get(n, 0))]

w, o = cascade_community_breakdown(G_lcc, seed_intra, node_comm)
total = w + o
print(f"Seed community: Community 1 (largest)")
print(f"Mean within-community infections: {w:.1f} ({100*w/total:.1f}%)")
print(f"Mean cross-community infections:  {o:.1f} ({100*o/total:.1f}%)")

Within-community infections: (%)    Cross-community: (%)

Using Gephi

Dataset: The Twitch Streamer Social Network (MUSAE) records mutual friendship ties among English-language Twitch streamers, with node-level attributes including total channel views, days active on the platform, partnership status, and a mature content flag. Published by Rozemberczki, B., Allen, C., and Sarkar, R. (2021). “Multi-Scale Attributed Node Embedding.” Journal of Complex Networks, 9(2).

Download: Navigate to the MUSAE GitHub repository: https://github.com/benedekrozemberczki/MUSAE

Under input/dataset/, download:

  • musae_ENGB_edges.csv — friendship edge list
  • musae_ENGB_target.csv — node attributes (views, partner, etc.)

Save both files to your working directory.

Analytical focus: This session treats the Twitch friendship network as a model information environment where friendships are the channels through which trends, audiences, and influence flow. You will use Gephi to map the structure of influence, identify which actors control information pathways, detect communities that represent distinct influence clusters, and assess whether network structure predicts real-world audience reach.

Deliverable: Two exported PNG maps (one styled by influence measure, one by community) plus a written assessment. Due at end of class.

Data Reference

Edge file (musae_ENGB_edges.csv): Two columns, from and to, each containing integer node IDs. Each row is a mutual friendship between two streamers. Total: approximately 35,324 edges among 7,126 nodes.

Target file (musae_ENGB_target.csv): One row per streamer. Key columns:

Column Type Description
new_id / id Integer Streamer node ID (matches edge file)
views Integer Cumulative channel view count
partner 0 / 1 Twitch Partner status (1 = partnered)
mature 0 / 1 Mature content flag (1 = adult content)
days Integer Days account has been active

Intelligence framing: Treat views as a ground-truth measure of real-world reach. Treat partner as a proxy for established influence (Twitch partners have met verified audience thresholds). Your goal is to determine how well structural network position predicts these real-world influence measures.

Part 1 (12 min) · Import Data into Gephi

Goal: Build the Twitch network in Gephi by importing the edge list, then enriching each node with the attribute data from the target file. Unlike formats such as GEXF, a raw CSV edge list carries no node attributes — they must be imported separately and joined in the Data Laboratory. This two-step import mirrors the workflow for any real intelligence dataset where relational data and attribute data arrive from different sources.

Gephi

File → New Project

Step 2 — Import the Edge List

Gephi

File → Import Spreadsheet → select musae_ENGB_edges.csv

In the Import Spreadsheet wizard:

  1. General options step:
    • Import as: Edges table
    • Separator: Comma
    • Check: “Has headers” (the file has from, to headers)
  2. Column assignment:
    • from → Source
    • to → Target
  3. Import settings: Graph type: Undirected
  4. → Finish

Part 2 (10 min) · Layout: Revealing Network Structure

Goal: Apply a force-directed layout that spatially organizes streamers so that those with more mutual friends are drawn together. In a network framed around information flow, spatial proximity in a force-directed layout approximates structural proximity — nodes that are close together are likely to exchange information quickly and frequently. The layout is therefore not just cosmetic: it encodes analytical meaning.

Step 5 — Apply ForceAtlas2

Gephi

Layout panel (left sidebar) → select ForceAtlas 2

Recommended settings for this network size (7,126 nodes):

  • Enable LinLog mode: produces cleaner cluster separation at the cost of more runtime
  • Enable Dissuade Hubs: pushes high-degree nodes toward their cluster periphery, making hub structure more visible
  • Scaling: 10.0
  • Gravity: 1.0
  • Approximate repulsion: enabled (faster on large graphs)

Click Run. Allow 90–120 seconds for the layout to converge. Watch the Overview canvas — the network should resolve from a compressed ball into distinct clusters. Click Stop when movement slows.

Step 6 — Prevent Overlap

Gephi

After ForceAtlas2 stabilizes:

Switch layout to Noverlap → click Run briefly (5 seconds) → Stop

This separates any node labels that overlap without disrupting the global cluster positions established by ForceAtlas2.

Step 7 — First Visual Impression

Before configuring any appearance settings, look at the layout and answer from visual inspection only.

Approximately how many distinct spatial clusters are visible?

Does the network have a clear dense core with a sparse periphery (core-periphery structure), or do clusters appear roughly equal in density?

Are there any visible “bridges” — thin chains of nodes connecting otherwise separate clusters?

In one sentence, describe the overall spatial impression of this network:

Part 3 (10 min) · Compute Influence Statistics

Goal: Run Gephi’s built-in statistics to compute network-level metrics and node-level influence scores. Run them in the order listed below. Each statistic adds a new column to the node table in Data Laboratory, which is then available for visual styling.

Note on betweenness: Betweenness centrality is computationally expensive for a 7,000-node network. Gephi uses a probabilistic approximation; set it running in the background while you work through other steps. The approximation is accurate enough for ranking purposes.

Step 8 — Run Statistics (in order)

Gephi

Statistics panel (right sidebar). Click Run next to each item and close the report window after recording the result.

  1. Average Degree → records result in status bar and adds Degree column.
  2. Network Diameter → computes diameter, average path length, and adds Betweenness Centrality and Closeness Centrality to the node table. This will take 1–3 minutes. Start it and proceed to Step 9 while it runs.
  3. PageRank → adds PageRank column. In the PageRank settings, set probability: 0.85. Fast (seconds).
  4. Graph Density → records density in the report.
  5. Connected Components → reports number of components.

Step 9 — Record Network-Level Results

Average degree
Network diameter
Avg path length
Graph density

Part 4 (12 min) · Visual Styling for Influence

Goal: Encode analytical findings visually using Gephi’s Appearance panel. You will build two versions of the map:

Map A — Structural influence: Node size = PageRank (recursive influence score). Node color = degree centrality (direct reach). This map answers: who is structurally most important for spreading information?

Map B — Ground-truth influence: Node size = views (actual audience reach). Node color = partner status (platform recognition). This map answers: where is real-world influence concentrated, and does it match structural position?

Comparing Maps A and B visually reveals whether structural importance and real-world influence are aligned or divergent — a core analytical question for any influence network.

Step 11 — Map A: Size by PageRank

Gephi

Appearance panel (top-left of Overview) → Nodes tab → Size icon (three circles):

  • Select Ranking → attribute: PageRank
  • Minimum size: 1   Maximum size: 20

→ Apply

Nodes now scale with their recursive influence score. The largest nodes are the most important hubs for network-wide information diffusion.

Step 12 — Map A: Color by Degree

Gephi

  • Classification: Spline interpolation (handles the skewed degree distribution better than linear)

→ Apply

Step 13 — Map A: Edge Styling

Gephi

→ Apply

Part 5 (8 min) · Community Detection and Influence Clusters

Goal: Detect communities using the Louvain modularity algorithm and assess whether communities correspond to distinct influence clusters — groups of streamers who are mutually embedded and whose audiences likely overlap. In information flow terms, a high-modularity community structure implies that information tends to circulate within communities before crossing to others — a finding with direct implications for targeted narrative operations.

Step 17 — Run Modularity

Gephi

Statistics panel → Modularity → Run

In the Modularity settings dialog:

  • Resolution: 1.0
  • Uncheck: “Use weights” (edges are unweighted)

→ OK

Part 6 (5 min) · Broker Identification: Bridges Between Communities

Goal: Identify the broker actors — nodes that connect otherwise separate communities and therefore control inter-community information flow. In influence network analysis, brokers are the actors most capable of carrying a narrative from one audience cluster to another. They are often more strategically valuable than pure hubs: a hub amplifies within its community, but a broker determines whether amplification crosses community boundaries.

Written Assessment (remaining time; complete as homework)

Write approximately 350–450 words addressing all four points.

  1. Structure vs. real-world influence: Based on your comparison of Maps A and B, does structural network position (PageRank, degree) predict real-world audience reach (views, partner status)? Identify at least one specific node where the two diverge significantly and explain what could account for the divergence. What does this tell an analyst who wants to use structural data as a proxy for real-world influence when ground-truth data is unavailable?

  2. Community structure and information containment: With a modularity score of [your value] and [N] communities, describe the community structure you found. Do communities appear to represent distinct influence clusters (e.g., groups of streamers with overlapping audiences)? Based on the modularity score, would you expect information to circulate primarily within communities before crossing to others, or would cross-community diffusion be frequent?

  3. Broker actors: Using your betweenness analysis, identify the role of broker actors in this influence network. Are the top-betweenness nodes also the top-degree or top-PageRank nodes, or is there a distinct set of structurally important brokers? In an influence operation, would you prioritize seeding a narrative through hubs (high degree/PageRank) or brokers (high betweenness)? Justify your answer with reference to what each measure captures.

  4. Visual encoding critique: Evaluate the visual design choices you made across your three maps. Which encoding (size/color combination) produced the most analytically informative map, and why? Is there an attribute or structural measure you computed that you did not visually encode but should have? What one change to your final map would most improve its utility as a product for a non-technical senior analyst?

Submit: Written assessment plus [LastName]_Twitch_MapA_Structural.png, [LastName]_Twitch_MapB_RealWorld.png, [LastName]_Twitch_Final.png, and [LastName]_Twitch_Influence.gephi.

Using i2 Analyst Notebook

Dataset: The Twitch Streamer Social Network (MUSAE) records mutual friendship ties among English-language Twitch streamers, with node-level attributes including total channel views, platform partnership status, mature content flag, and account longevity (days active). Published by Rozemberczki, B., Allen, C., and Sarkar, R. (2021). “Multi-Scale Attributed Node Embedding.” Journal of Complex Networks, 9(2).

Files provided: twitch_top200_entities.csv and twitch_top200_links.csv. These files contain the 200 most degree-central streamers in the English-language network and all friendship links between them — a subgraph that preserves the network’s core structure at a size appropriate for i2 Analyst Notebook.

Analytical focus: This session treats the Twitch friendship network as a model information environment and uses i2 to answer an influence mapping question: among the platform’s most connected streamers, who controls information pathways, who has genuine audience reach, and do those two populations overlap? You will build a link chart, classify streamers by influence tier, run structural analysis, and produce a briefable product identifying the network’s most analytically significant actors.

Deliverable: One exported annotated i2 chart image, one saved ego network chart, and a written assessment. All due at end of class.

Data Reference

File Column Description
entities.csv label Display label formatted as “Streamer [ID]”
node_id Integer node identifier
views Cumulative total channel view count
partner Twitch Partner status: 1 = partnered, 0 = not
mature Mature content flag: 1 = adult content
days Days since account creation
degree Number of friendships in the full network
tier Influence tier: “Mega” ($>\(1M views), "Established" (100K–1M), "Emerging" (\)<$100K)
links.csv source Source streamer label (e.g., “Streamer 42”)
target Target streamer label
link_type Always “Friendship” (mutual, undirected)

Influence tier thresholds:

Mega-influencers (\(>\) 1,000,000 views): Large icon, gold fill. Established audience; likely recognizable within the platform community.

Established streamers (100,000 – 1,000,000 views): Medium icon, green fill. Significant but not platform-dominant audience.

Emerging streamers (\(<\) 100,000 views): Small icon, grey fill. Structurally well-connected (they appear in this dataset because of their high degree) but with limited current audience reach.

  • Small grey entity = Emerging streamer ($<$100K views)
  • Purple double border = Twitch Partner (platform-verified)
  • Purple light line = Mutual friendship link
  • Entity size also reflects betweenness centrality (from i2 SNA visualization)

Analytical note: “[N] Mega-influencers, [M] Twitch Partners identified among top-200 degree nodes. Top structural actor by betweenness: [Streamer ID], [tier], betweenness = [score].”

INSTRUCTOR NOTES — Not for student distribution

Data Preparation (Complete Before Class)

Run the following Python script to generate the two CSV files students need. Requires pandas and the two raw MUSAE files (musae_ENGB_edges.csv and musae_ENGB_target.csv) downloaded from the MUSAE GitHub repository.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

edges  = pd.read_csv('musae_ENGB_edges.csv')
target = pd.read_csv('musae_ENGB_target.csv')

# Standardise node ID column name
id_col = 'new_id' if 'new_id' in target.columns else 'id'
target = target.rename(columns={id_col: 'node_id'})

# Compute degree in full network
from collections import Counter
deg = Counter()
for _, row in edges.iterrows():
    deg[row['from']] += 1
    deg[row['to']]   += 1
target['degree'] = target['node_id'].map(deg).fillna(0).astype(int)

# Select top 200 by degree
top200 = target.nlargest(200, 'degree')['node_id'].tolist()

# Assign influence tiers
def tier(v):
    if v > 1_000_000: return 'Mega'
    if v > 100_000:   return 'Established'
    return 'Emerging'
target['tier'] = target['views'].apply(tier)

# Build entity file
entities = target[target['node_id'].isin(top200)].copy()
entities['label'] = 'Streamer ' + entities['node_id'].astype(str)
entities[['label','node_id','views','partner',
          'mature','days','degree','tier']].to_csv(
    'twitch_top200_entities.csv', index=False)

# Build link file: only edges where both endpoints in top200
top200_set = set(top200)
links = edges[(edges['from'].isin(top200_set)) &
              (edges['to'].isin(top200_set))].copy()
links['source'] = 'Streamer ' + links['from'].astype(str)
links['target'] = 'Streamer ' + links['to'].astype(str)
links['link_type'] = 'Friendship'
links[['source','target','link_type']].to_csv(
    'twitch_top200_links.csv', index=False)

print(f"Entities: {len(entities)}")
print(f"Links:    {len(links)}")

Test before class. Open the two CSV files in i2 following Steps 2 and 3 and verify that all links match existing entities (no floating endpoints).

Expected Values

Subgraph size: 200 entities; typically 1,800–3,200 links in the top-200 subgraph (approximately 9–16 average connections per entity within the subgraph, noting that these 200 nodes were selected by full-network degree so they are mutually well-connected).

Influence tier distribution (approximate): Mega ($>\(1M views): 15–30 nodes. Established (100K–1M): 60–90 nodes. Emerging (\)<$100K): 90–120 nodes. Note: many high-degree streamers have not converted structural centrality into large audiences — this is the key analytical tension.

Partner rate in top-200 subgraph: Approximately 25–40%, substantially higher than the platform-wide 8–12%. Structural centrality and partnership co-occur more often than chance, but the relationship is far from deterministic.

Top betweenness actor: In most dataset versions, the top-betweenness actor in the top-200 subgraph belongs to the Established tier (not the Mega tier). This is the primary analytical teaching moment: the actor with the largest structural control over information flow is not the one with the largest audience.

Cluster count: Students will typically identify 4–7 clusters visually. The actual Louvain community count (computed in Gephi, not available natively in i2) is approximately 8–15. Expect student zone counts to be lower because i2’s manual grouping merges small communities.

Label-Matching Issue

The critical pre-class check: the source and target columns in the link CSV use the format “Streamer 42”, and the label column in the entity CSV uses the same format. If these do not match exactly (case, space, format), links will be unmatched. Verify by importing both files into i2 before class and checking the status bar for unmatched link count.

Common i2 Errors

“Select by Attributes” not finding Tier values: Occurs when the tier column was not mapped to an attribute during entity import (mapped to “Ignore” instead). Fix: clear all entities and re-import with correct column mapping.

SNA module giving zero values: Occurs when the chart has no links (link import failed or mismatched). Check: right-click any entity and see if any links appear in the context menu. If not, re-import links with correct label matching.

“New from Selection” not preserving appearance: Some i2 versions do not carry appearance settings to the new chart. Instruct students to reapply tier colors in the ego network chart if this occurs — it takes 2–3 minutes with the select-by-attribute method from Part 2.

Analytical Discussion Anchors

The Emerging-tier broker phenomenon: In most network configurations, the top-betweenness actor in the top-200 subgraph has substantially fewer views than the top-degree actor. Ask: “If you were an information operations analyst trying to seed a narrative, would you approach the actor with the most followers or the actor with the highest betweenness? What is the difference in what each type of actor can do for you?”

Partner status as ground truth: Partner status represents formal platform recognition that a streamer has met audience thresholds. It is therefore more reliable than raw view counts (which can include bot views, viral one-time events, etc.). Ask: “Do the top structural actors have partner status? If not, what does it mean that the platform has not formally recognized the structurally most important actors in this network?”

i2 limitations for this dataset: The Twitch dataset has no temporal edge data (friendship timestamps are not available in MUSAE). Students will note that i2’s timeline integration — one of its primary advantages — cannot be used here. This is a productive constraint: it shows students when i2 is and is not the right tool. The “days active” attribute can be used as a rough account-longevity proxy, but it is a node attribute, not an edge timestamp.

Scalability limitation: The full 7,126-node Twitch ENGB network cannot be practically analyzed in i2 (too many entities for the chart canvas and SNA module). This motivates the top-200 subgraph approach and illustrates why Python and Gephi are necessary for large-scale network analysis — i2 is an analyst tool, not a computational one. This distinction is worth stating explicitly.
